rules.heading: Skills
rules.text: Skills are the heart of the Dungeon Crawler Carl Roleplaying Game. You make Skill Checks to do most things and gain upgrades from ranking up Skills. Each Skill entry follows a consistent format: The header is the name that tells you exactly what it’s called—hopefully something that sounds impressive when shouted aloud. Under the header is a list of keywords identifying the Stat Mod you add to the Skill Check, if any, and any special traits tied to the Skill. The description explains what the Skill actually does, which you should probably read before attempting it. On average, 35.71% of deaths in past Crawls are attributable to illiteracy. The description may contain additional keywords like “AI Favor” and “Limitations,” which vary by the Skill type. Finally, the entry teases you with upgrade benefits if you train it to higher Ranks, as if you need more incentive to avoid your leg being ripped off by a giant demon crab, only to wake up two floors later to discover it grew an eyeball and a mouth and is licking your face off in anger at being replaced by a prosthetic.

rules.heading: Skill Checks
rules.text: Skill Checks are either Opposed or Unopposed, depending on what you are up against (see p. 59). Roll 1d20, add your Skill’s Rank, and add your associated Stat Mod. If the total matches or exceeds the Difficulty of the Check, the outcome is at least a Standard Success but could grant even better effects if you significantly exceed the Difficulty. Your GM determines the Difficulty for a Check, so they’re the one who needs to know the exact type of Skill Check you’re making. They won’t share the Difficulty with you but will only inform you of the outcome. Don’t worry, System AIs don’t cheat or lie; we always fully believe what we tell you. But if you must know every detail (good for you, boring for viewers), Opposed Skills make Checks against a specific antagonist, and the Difficulty factors in their Stat Mod. Unopposed Skills make Checks against things that don’t have a Stat block, like objects or the environment. The Skill’s description lists the effects of a Standard Success. Lots of results are possible other than a Standard Success (see Degrees of Success and Failure, p. 60). Know that I encourage GMs to get creative when narrating both Successes and Fails; the more spectacular the results (good or bad), the more the viewers can’t turn away.

rules.heading: Passive Skills
rules.text: You don’t make Skill Checks to gain the effects of Passive Skills. This makes them easy to use but hard to Rank-up; since you don’t make a Skill Check, you can’t mark it for a Skill Advancement Check (p. 169). Each Passive Skill entry describes how you can increase its Rank, typically requiring magic gear and training, though some feature other ways. Using a Passive Skill typically requires an Action like any other Skill type. However, some trigger alongside other Skills at no extra Action cost, like Hand-to-Hand Damage Effects (see p. 180). You can’t use a Passive Skill if you have no Ranks in it (untrained). The easiest way to gain them is via a potion, scroll, or gear. They can also be found in some Race and Class benefits starting on the Third Floor.

rules.heading: Skill Upgrades
rules.text: As Skills increase in Rank, they grant additional bonuses at Ranks 5, 10, and 15. add extra damage dice to the base effect damage, and these always apply even if other parts of the Upgrade are situational. Where an Upgrade increases the range or duration, removes a limitation, or the like, the Upgrade overrides the base effect instead of being in addition to it. All other sorts of Upgrades get added together. Typically, these additive Upgrades use a plus sign (+) to help note this.

rules.heading: Creating Your Own Skills
rules.text: The list of Skills in the World Dungeon is endless. Our artificial sky’s the limit, folks! Here’s the framework in which you can create any Skill you want. You’ll need to use it if you come across a Skill or Spell marked with an gear asterisk ( ): that’s the cue that it’s a Custom Skill not found in this book. The simplest way to customize a Skill is to reuse an existing Skill but reframe its narrative. A Skill like Dumpster Diving could just as easily become Search 4 174 Copyright Renegade Game Studios. Unauthorized distribution prohibited. 08/25/2026. just by changing the name and thematic focus while still operating within the same mechanical structure. Mixing and matching Skill effects and Upgrades is a great way to create weird Skills to really customize your crawler. A Crochet Skill, for instance, might have a custom Upgrade that works like a Utility Skill Upgrade, or it could borrow a Rank 5 Upgrade found on the Dagger Skill. You can invent a new effect or Upgrade following the guideline that the more niche it is, the stronger it can be. If something ends up too strong or too weak, the GM can always patch it later. The system adjusts; so should you. In play, you’ll often find more than one Skill that applies to a situation. Because Skills improve through use, you might choose to attempt a task with a weaker or less-optimal Skill just to gain experience with it. This is perfectly normal behavior and occa-sionally even works out. Made-up Skills should typically be narrowly focused and should not completely replace or outgun existing Skills… or Actions like Evade. If you want to create an Evade-like Skill, it should perhaps only be useful against a certain attack type (such as Edged Weapons and Ranged Weapons) or come with a significant downside that makes its usage situational. Evade Checks don’t use Ranks, so anything that adds Ranks to a Skill Check that lets you avoid any type of attack will instantly be much better than Evading, and that’s a no-no. If you don’t spill blood, I won’t be happy. That’s the whole point!

rules.heading: Attack Skills (Weapons)
rules.text: Attack Skills represent your ability to harm, disable, or otherwise make something stop trying to kill you, whether through weapons, fists, or pure destructive intent. Name: The name of the Attack appears as a headline to the entry. Attack Type: Melee or Ranged. Most Attacks are Melee, which have a range of 5 feet (i.e., adjacent). If an Attack has a range farther than that, it will be noted in the Range entry below this line. The default Stat Mod used for Melee rolls to hit is Str, while the default Stat Mod for ranged weapon Attacks is Dex. If another Stat Mod is used to hit, it will be listed here. Range: If the Attack can hit a target farther than 5 feet away, the maximum distance it can hit will be listed here. If the Attack has no range listed, its range is Melee range (adjacent or within 5 feet). AI Favor: Low-damage weapons grant AI Favor to you if you use such a wimpy Attack for a majority of your attacks during a combat that lasts for at least three rounds. Limitations: Any conditions, requirements, or penalties are listed here. “Requires two hands to wield” is a common limitation, which means both hands must be used to wield the weapon (I’m sure you never would’ve figured that out without this explanation). You can’t hold other things at the same time when attacking. If the weapon or effect has a cooldown, it will be listed here. Hit or miss, the timer starts. While on cooldown, the weapon or effect cannot be used. Description: Any notes or descriptions of the Skill are listed here. Make an Attack Skill Check vs. the target’s Evade value, which is: 10 + Dex + the Floor number. Base Damage: This is the damage dice the weapon deals with 0–4 Ranks in the Skill. Zero Ranks means using it untrained. The appropriate Stat Mod value is added to the damage. This Mod does not always match the one listed in the Attack Type line, and not every weapon adds a Stat Mod. Finally, the damage type is listed. The damage type is important if the target has Resistance, Immunity, or Vulnerability to that damage type. Effects: If there are effects other than damage, they will be listed there. Upgrades: When you reach Rank 5, 10, and 15, these bonuses kick in. Write your Attack Skills in the “Attacks” section on the front of your character sheet. Fill out the “To Hit” box for your weapons, writing in your “Rank + Stat Mod” values. Then fill in the “Damage” box. Write in the dice as “1dX,” replacing the “X” with the die type noted in the description. The weapon’s base damage entry will also tell you which Stat Mod (if any) you add to the damage. Use the Effects area to write in short reminders of base effects, Upgrade effects, and AI Favor (if any). Lastly, write in the Attack Skill name on your “Skills” list. There, you can write in additional notes and mark the advancement box on the far right when you use the Skill. This keeps all your Skills in one place when rolling for Skill Advancement (p. 169). Just remember to update your Rank in the “Attacks” section as well when you advance an Attack Skill, or you’ll be weak forever, just like your middle school gym teacher prophesied.

rules.heading: Explosives Skills
rules.text: For handling explosives, see Explosives Handling, Goblin Explosives, and Incendiary Device Handling in Utility Skills (below). These Skills will also be useful for crafting your own explosives once you have access to a Sapper’s Table on the Fourth Floor. As crawlers descend to lower floors, explosives become more complex than the Tutorial Floors’ “light and throw” variety. See the Area of Effect Attacks (p. 83) for targeting, Difficulties, and what happens when you miss your target with tossed explosives. Your explosives Skill is not used when attacking with a thrown explosive, but the GM should have you make an Unopposed handling Skill Check before throwing. Here are the explosives typically found on the first five floors. Lesser explosives can be found on lower floors, but the more powerful explosives are rarely seen on the upper floors. Floor 1: Standard Explosive—Dynamite: 1d6 Bludgeoning, 0ft Blast radius +5ft Splash. Floor 2: Goblin Explosive—Dynamite: 2d6 Bludgeoning damage, 5ft Blast radius + 5ft Splash. Floor 2: Incendiary Device—Carl’s Jug O’ Boom: 1d8 Fire damage, 5ft Blast radius + 15ft Splash. Anyone who loses at least 1 Health Bar slot gains the Burned Debuff. Floor 3: Goblin Explosive—Hob-Lobbers: 3d6 Piercing, +10ft Splash Floor 4: Standard Explosive—Demon Det Cord: 5d6 Bludgeoning, deals double damage to objects. Can only be applied to non-moving targets. Floor 5: Incendiary Device—Gnomish Knock-Knock: 4d6 Fire, 10ft Blast radius +10ft Splash, and anyone who fails to Evade gains the Burned Debuff. As this is a notoriously unstable fuel-air explosive, a Critical Fail is achieved on a Natural 1–4. Most explosives are custom made and not available on store shelves. Carl had his custom Jelly Bombs, Banger Spheres, Chum Bombs, and more.

rules.heading: Smoke
rules.text: Smoke is used for concealment, distraction, and confusion. Attacking into or out of smoke is done with Disadvantage (see Mob Advantage and Disadvantage p. 60). Thrown smoke bombs are popular on most dungeon floors as a way to get out of trouble quick-ly. See the Throwing Skill (p. 200) for targeting, Difficulties, and what happens when you miss your target. You don’t need to make a Skill Check to drop it in your own space. Floor 1: Goblin Smoke Bomb: Creates a multicolor smoke cloud that reaches 30 feet in each direction from the point of impact, with a maximum duration of 3 minutes. However, even a slight breeze will dissipate it in 1 minute. Floor 3: Hobgoblin Smoke Curtain: Creates a dense white fog over a 60ft radius that holds even in a breeze. Floor 5: Hobgoblin Disco Ball: Created by infusing (see Infusion Skill, p. 194) an Invisibility potion onto a Hobgoblin Smoke Curtain. It produces thick multi-hued smoke plumes, along with some sick beats. It blinds everyone in the area, friend and foe alike.

rules.heading: Utility Skills
rules.text: Utility Skills help crawlers survive, adapt, and solve problems that can’t be fixed by hitting them until they stop moving. Checks that are labeled as Unopposed can, at the GM’s discretion, become Opposed if something is actively working against you. For example, you’re trying to swim the rapids, and some dipshit is throwing fishing nets at you. Cut it out, Cletus! Or I’m gonna tell Mom on you!

skills.name: Escape Artist
skills.description:
Holy Houdini! While anyone can use Dexterity to wiggle out of restraints or a hold, you’re especially skilled at the art of escape. When you try to escape from bonds or being Held, you can use this Skill.

When trying to escape bonds, make an Unopposed Skill Check.

To escape being Held, make a Str-Opposed Skill Check. Based on the complexity or simplicity of what binds you, the GM may have you make the Check with Advantage or Disadvantage.

On Success, you escape your bonds or the creature holding you.

upgrades.5: You can escape your bonds, and no one sees you do it. If you escape being Held, you can then take a Step (also unseen).
upgrades.10: When other crawlers in your party roll this skill untrained, they roll as normal (not with Disadvantage).
upgrades.15: When you slip out, you may immediately take an Action with Advantage.

skills.limitations: After 1 minute of Swimming (Success or Fail) or immediately on a Major Fail or worse, gain the Fatigued Debuff.

skills.limitations: A crawler may attempt this Skill Check only once per combat.
skills.description:

On Success, you and each member of your party gain a +1 bonus to Checks for the chosen discipline. Increase the bonus by +1 for each higher degree of Success.

upgrades.10: After using this Skill during a combat, you roll 2d10 when you Call a Play (still choose one die).
upgrades.15: The bonus applies to all three combat disciplines instead of just one.

skills.name: Throwing
skills.description:
This Skill is used for passing the pigskin with your pops or throwing dynamite (potentially also at your pops).

You can Throw an object that weighs up to your Str in pounds at a distance of up to your Str ×10 feet. If you want to Throw a heavier or bulkier item (up to the GM’s discretion), you do so with Disadvantage.

To hit a target area, make an Unopposed Skill Check.

To hit a foe with an object, make an Attack Skill Check vs. the target’s Evade.

On Success, you hit the target. On Fail, roll 1d8 for direction (see Figure 3). The amount the Skill Check missed by is the distance away in feet it lands.

upgrades.5: You have Advantage when Throwing to a target who wants to catch what you are selling.
upgrades.10: Choose the direction on a miss, rather than roll.
upgrades.15: Your Throw range is your Str ×20 feet.

Factors such as how long ago the tracks were made, the ground conditions, and whether other tracks or marks obscure them may influence the Difficulty. On Success, you either find the tracks or continue following them.
